deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT. The heading reads 'Berechnung der Bahn der Vesta aus vier Oertern' (computation of the orbit of Vesta from four places). Vesta was discovered by Olbers at Bremen on 1807 March 29. The page therefore dates from mid-to-late 1807, even though the bundle is labelled 1805. The page is the data-reduction stage. It prepares four geocentric ecliptic places of Vesta (α, β) and the corresponding Sun places and radii (Earth longitudes l = ☉+180°, log R) for an orbit determination. The next page continues the same scheme for observations III and IV. It then tabulates l, l', l'', l''' and α, α', α'', α''' and starts the orbit solution (quantities P', Q', P'', Q'', log a', b', etc.).

1. OBSERVATIONS (table at top). Each row gives the local mean time, the place, the observed right ascension α_obs and declination δ_obs, a geocentric distance Δ, the 'Aberrationszeit' (light time) and the 'Reductio ad meridianum' (longitude difference from Paris):
- I: 1807 Mar 30, 12h33m17s, Bremen; α = 183°52'41", δ = 11°54'27"; Δ = 1.2833; light time 633 s; longitude 25m51s.
- II: May 3, 9h11m05s, Milan ('Mayland'); α = 178°35'4.2", δ = 12°42'10.0"; Δ = 1.4424; 711 s; 27m25s.
- III: Jun 6, 11h01m55s, Bremen; α = 180°57'5", δ = 9°10'28"; Δ = 1.7602; 868 s; 25m51s.
- IV: Jul 11, 10h30m19s, Lilienthal; α = 189°49'7.7", δ = 3°9'10.1"; Δ = 2.1299; 1050 s; 26m16s.
The light time is τ = 493 s·Δ, i.e. Delambre's 493.2 s per AU (checks: 1.2833·493.2 = 632.9; 2.1299·493.2 = 1050.5).

2. TIME REDUCTION (my explicit restatement). Paris time corrected for aberration is t_P = t_local − (longitude difference) − τ.
- I: 12:33:17 − 0:25:51 − 0:10:33 = 11:56:53.
- II: 9:11:05 − 0:27:25 − 0:11:51 = 8:31:49.
- III: 11:01:55 − 0:25:51 − 0:14:28 = 10:21:36.
- IV: 10:30:19 − 0:26:16 − 0:17:30 = 9:46:33.
These are converted to decimal minutes, then hours, then days. They are counted as 'März' day numbers: Mar 30.497836, Mar 64.355428 (May 3), Mar 98.431667 (Jun 6), Mar 133.407326 (Jul 11). Taken relative to the epoch 'Mittag 31 März' (Paris mean noon, March 31) they become −0.502164, +33.355428, +67.431667, +102.407326 days.
The logarithms of these intervals are 9.7008456, 1.5231665, 1.8288639, 2.0103311. log of the daily precession is 9.1372475, i.e. 50.1"/365.25 = 0.137175" per day. From these follow the precession corrections −0.07", +4.58", +9.25", +14.05". They are used on the next page to reduce all longitudes to the mean equinox of 1807 March 31.0.

3. SUN PLACES ('Sonnenörter'), from solar tables with argument columns M A B C D E F N (perturbation arguments).

Obs I:
- Epoch mean longitude 9s9°42'23.5" (+0.4").
- Motion 2s27°43'21.4" and a further −7.7" give mean longitude 7°25'38.6" as written.
- Perigee 9s9°36'17" + 15" = 9s9°36'32".
- Equation of centre +1°54'41.3".
- Nutation +17.0".
- Moon 0.1" and 0.2"; Venus 6.2"; Mars 5.1"; Jupiter 25.3"; Saturn 0.9".
- +20.2" removes the aberration built into the tables, giving the true geometric longitude.
- Result ☉ = 9°21'34.9".

Radius vector for obs I:
- Tabular value 0.9995427, plus perturbation corrections 387, 240, 156, 193, 25 (units of 1e−7), gives R = 0.9996428.
- log R = 9.9998448.

Obliquity for obs I: 23°27'53.4" − 2.80" + 0.3" = 23°27'50.9".

Obs II:
- 9s9°42'23.9" + 4s0°14'56.2" + 50'35.3" = 1s10°47'55.4" (mean longitude).
- Perigee 9s9°36'38"; the mean anomaly noted is 4s1°11.29'.
- Equation of centre +1°36'56.2".
- Nutation +16.1"; Moon +2.0"; Venus 8.3"; Mars 4.2"; Jupiter 23.1"; Saturn 0.4"; +20.2".
- Result ☉ = 42°26'5.9".
- Radius 1.0087995, plus corrections 651, 104, 144, 291, 24, gives R = 1.0089209 and log R = 0.0038571.
- Obliquity 23°27'53.4" − 3.1" − 0.1" = 23°27'50.2".

The argument columns are summed mod 1000. Most sums can be verified, e.g. B 277+244 = 521; N 284+13 = 297; D 367+178 = 545.

4. PARALLAX. In the right-hand block of obs II:
- log 8.6" (solar horizontal parallax) = 0.93450.
- log(1/Δ) = 9.84091, with Δ = 1.4424.
- φ_Milan = 45°27'57" and δ = 12°42'10", so φ−δ = 32°45'47" and log sin(φ−δ) = 9.73333.
- Sum 0.50874 gives a parallax in declination of 3.23". Hence δ' = 12°42'10.0" + 3.23" = 12°42'13.23".
- The figures 40°48'32" + 134°48'30" = 175°37'2" appear to be sidereal time at noon plus the light-time-corrected local time 8h59m14s in degrees. This gives the local sidereal time, showing the hour angle is only about −3°, so the RA parallax is negligible. This interpretation is mine.

For obs I the same reduction gives δ = 11°54'27" + 4.42" = 11°54'31.42": with φ_Bremen ≈ 53°05', 8.6·sin(41.2°)/1.2833 ≈ 4.41". It also gives α = 183°52'41.66" (+0.66" RA parallax).

5. EQUATORIAL → ECLIPTIC CONVERSION, via the auxiliary angle N:
- tan N = tan δ / sin α.
- tan λ = tan α · cos(N−ε) / cos N.
- tan β = tan(N−ε) · sin λ.

Obs I (α = 183°52'41.66", δ = 11°54'31.42", ε = 23°27'50.9"):
- log tan α = 8.8311759; log sin|α−180°| = 8.8301802; log tan δ = 9.3240604.
- N = 107°46'54.64" (second quadrant, since sin α < 0); N−ε = 84°19'3.74".
- log cos(N−ε) = 8.9956889; log|cos N| = 9.4848599.
- log tan(λ−180°) = 8.3420049 (sign negative), so λ = 178°44'27.27".
- log sin = 8.3419000; log tan(N−ε) = 1.0021718.
- log tan β = 9.3440718, so β = 12°27'11.35".

Obs II (α = 178°35'4.20", δ = 12°42'13.23", ε = 23°27'50.2"):
- log tan = 8.3928756; log sin = 8.3927431; log tan δ = 9.3530062.
- N = 83°44'47.04"; N−ε = 60°16'56.84".
- log cos(N−ε) = 9.6952405; log cos N = 9.0371449.
- log tan(180°−λ) = 9.0509712, so λ = 173°35'1.93".
- log sin = 9.0482425; log tan(N−ε) = 0.2435192.
- log tan β = 9.2917617, so β = 11°4'37.53".

Side columns (94491, 5117198, 9896601*, 107636, 9918326*, 6554994, 6580956, 0.6580956) are control computations. Among them are log cos β = 9.9896601 (obs I) and 9.9918326 (obs II, carried to the next page). Their exact role is not fully certain.

6. ON THE NEXT PAGE these become, after subtracting nutation and adding precession:
- l = ☉+180° − nutation + precession: 189°21'34.9" − 17.0" + 0.07" = 189°21'17.97"; 222°26'5.9" − 16.1" − 4.58" = 222°25'45.22".
- α (ecliptic longitude) = 178°44'27.27" − 17.0" + 0.07" ≈ 178°44'10.3"; 173°35'1.93" − 16.1" − 4.58" = 173°34'41.25".
- β = 12°27'11.35" for obs I. For obs II the value is written 11°4'37.53".
This confirms that the page's purpose is to supply reduced, light-time-corrected heliocentric Earth places and geocentric ecliptic places for the four-observation orbit solution.
errors: Obs I mean solar longitude: 9s9°42'23.5" + 0.4" + 2s27°43'21.4" − 7.7" gives 7°25'37.6", but 7°25'38.6" is written. The interval check against obs II (33.857592 d × 0.98564734°/d = 33°22'17.9") agrees with 37.6", so this is probably a 1" slip. It could also be a misreading of the −7.7 (−6.7?).

The local sidereal time for the Milan parallax (175°37'2") seems to be formed from the light-time-corrected time 8h59m14s and without the solar-to-sidereal acceleration. The effect on a ~3" parallax is negligible, so this is not a real error.

The lunar terms in the radius vector (387, 651 units of 1e−7) look larger than the true lunar effect (~300 max). The symbol may mark a different table term; the reading is uncertain, not demonstrably an error.
All other checked steps (time reductions, decimal conversions, logarithms, N, N−ε, λ, β, log R, parallax 3.23") are correct to the last place.

results.what: Reduction of observation times to Paris meridian and correction for light time τ = 493.2 s·Δ.
results.usually_credited_to: Standard 18th-century practice (Bradley/Delambre constants); systematised in Gauss, Theoria Motus (1809) §118

results.what: Sun places from solar tables with planetary perturbations, nutation and removal of tabular aberration; log of Earth–Sun distance.
results.modern_name: Solar ephemeris computation / heliocentric Earth position

results.what: Diurnal parallax in declination, 8.6"·sin(φ−δ)/Δ, near the meridian.
Conversion of (α, δ) to ecliptic (λ, β) via the auxiliary angle N: tan N = tan δ/sin α, tan λ = tan α·cos(N−ε)/cos N, tan β = tan(N−ε)·sin λ.
Data preparation for determining Vesta's orbit from four observations (1807).
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss, Vesta orbits published in von Zach's Monatliche Correspondenz 1807

deep.surprise_reason: This is routine reduction work for Gauss's well-documented 1807 Vesta orbit computations. The only mild point of interest is the dating: the content is from 1807 though filed under 1805.
